source.title: Resource-Constrained Knowledge Diffusion Processes Inspired by Human Peer Learning
source.authors: Ehsan Beikihassan; Amy K. Hoover; Ioannis Koutis; Alipanah Parviz; Niloofar Aghaieabiane

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests random-label memorization and noisy-label robustness in a peer-learning population, using a different training process from the original claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own random-label and noisy-label experiments in Section 3.4. The cited Zhang et al. result is prior work and is not recorded as this study's result. Other values in the figures are not transcribed as numbers.
record.test_reason: The single-model LeNet experiment directly measures random-label fitting in a new architecture–dataset setting. The peer-learning experiments evaluate a different population training procedure, and the noisy-label experiment reports test accuracy without establishing perfect training fit or a trend across noise fractions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' interpretation: POM appears resistant to random-label memorization, and POM/RGBT show robustness to 40% noisy labels. Their stronger claim that the modular population lacks memorization capacity exceeds what finite training runs establish; the paper itself calls for further investigation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses populations of identical-architecture learners trained through teacher-provided pseudolabels and grouping policies; random-label and noisy-label results are not a reproduction of the original single-network training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Random-label memorization differs across training policy: the single LeNet and RGBT show above-chance accuracy, while POM stays near chance. Under 40% label noise, behavior differs between POM/RGBT and the noisy-Oracle comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: RGBT reaches about 35% random-label training accuracy, while POM remains at 10–11%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-label memorization in peer-trained populations depends on the grouping and teaching policy.

fits_no_version.finding: At 40% label noise, POM and RGBT show little overfitting and later self-correction, while direct noisy-Oracle training loses almost 30% test accuracy after 600 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Peer-learning policies can reduce late test-performance deterioration under fixed label corruption.

record.problems: Random-label results are reported for LeNet, and the noisy-label comparison is a single ResNet experiment at 40% noise. The paper describes the random-label and noisy-label plots in text but does not provide uncertainty for those specific results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant results left out. Cited prior-work results were excluded.

untested.parts: Chance test performance on random labels, matched true-label training with unchanged hyperparameters, and eventual near-zero training error beyond the reported training duration.
Training time for fitting random versus true labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian inputs.
Perfect training fit across noise fractions and steadily degrading test performance from clean to fully random labels.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Direct measurement of learning shared real-label patterns before memorizing noisy labels. The noisy-label test-accuracy trajectory alone does not establish that ordering.

record.verdict_notes: The slower RGBT memorization rate is a comparison between training policies, not random versus real labels as required by V2. The real-label-first discussion in Section 1.4 cites prior work; this study does not directly track fitting of clean versus corrupted labels.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish that standard networks reach zero or near-zero training error with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters while also having test error at chance and generalizing well on true labels.
Tests one noise fraction (40%) and reports behavior for selected policies; does not test a sweep from no noise to all noise or establish steadily rising test error while training remains perfect.

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained on a completely randomly labeled training set
rows.note: The paper says this is much higher than random expectation, but it is not zero or near-zero training error.
rows.check: The reported roughly 40% training accuracy establishes incomplete memorization, far below near-perfect fitting. It does not establish a capacity ceiling or eventual convergence.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, Architectures and Datasets; Section 3.4, Memorization; Figure 10(a).

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained under the Random-Groups Best-Teachers (RGBT) policy on randomly labeled data
rows.note: The authors describe memorization as taking place, but at a slower rate and to a lower value.
rows.check: This is performance under the study's RGBT population training procedure, rather than a standard individual network trained directly on fixed random labels. Identify the subject as a LeNet population and clarify whether the plotted accuracy is ensemble or average learner accuracy; the supplied text does not resolve that metric.

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained under the Planted Oracle Mechanism (POM) on randomly labeled data
rows.note: The authors say training accuracy stays near chance and interpret this as resistance to memorization.
rows.check: The 10–11% result concerns POM population training with changing peer pseudolabels, outside V1's standard-network setup. Identify the population-level subject and clarify the accuracy aggregation.

rows.subject: ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained using POM with randomly corrupted training labels
rows.value: very little overfitting; overfitting episodes occur after 600 epochs, followed by self-correcting behavior
rows.note: The paper reports a single experiment and does not establish the version's full noise-fraction trend or perfect training fit.
rows.check: Test-accuracy robustness at one noise fraction does not measure V4's perfect training fit or degradation across noise fractions. The subject is a ResNet population under POM, and the accuracy aggregation is unspecified in the supplied text.

rows.subject: ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained using RGBT with randomly corrupted training labels
rows.value: very little overfitting; overfitting episodes occur after 600 epochs, followed by self-correcting behavior
rows.note: The paper reports a single experiment and does not establish the version's full noise-fraction trend or perfect training fit.
rows.check: Test-accuracy robustness at one noise fraction does not measure V4's perfect training fit or degradation across noise fractions. The subject is a ResNet population under RGBT, and the accuracy aggregation is unspecified in the supplied text.

rows.subject: ResNet
rows.operation_detail: All models learn from the noisy Oracle
rows.value: test accuracy dropped almost 30% due to overfitting which started after 600 epochs
rows.note: Comparator condition reported by the authors for the noisy-label experiment.
rows.check: The almost 30% test-accuracy drop is a temporal overfitting result at fixed 40% noise, not V4's trend across noise fractions. No training-fit measurement establishes memorization of the corrupted labels, and the text does not clarify whether the drop is relative or in percentage points.

relationships.condition: Single toy LeNet trained on randomly labeled Fashion-MNIST, within the reported training run
relationships.reason: R1 reaches roughly 40% training accuracy versus 10% chance: substantial memorization, but clearly incomplete fitting rather than near-zero training error.
relationships.display_finding: Training accuracy reached roughly 40%, exceeding 10% chance accuracy but leaving fitting substantially incomplete.
